*Discrete Applied Mathematics* 89(1–3), 3–44, 1998.

## Context

The main results first appeared in a 1974 Carnegie Mellon technical report and were
published as an invited paper in 1998.
The paper treats *disjunctive programs*: linear programs with logical
("or") conditions on the constraints. Pure and mixed 0–1 programs are a special case.

## Main contributions

**1. Two descriptions of the convex hull.**

- An **extended (lifted) description** that adds one copy of the variables per term of the
  disjunction. This is the hull formulation explained in
  [Big-M vs. the Convex Hull](../big-m-vs-hull.qmd). It gives an LP whose projection is the
  convex hull, so a disjunctive program can be solved as one (possibly large) LP.
- A description in the **original variables**, in terms of the facets of the hull.

**2. Valid inequalities and facets.** Every valid inequality for the disjunctive set can be
derived from the disjuncts with suitable multipliers. The paper gives necessary and
sufficient conditions for such an inequality to define a facet. This is the theoretical
basis for **disjunctive cuts**.

**3. Sequential convexification.** For a class of problems called *facial* disjunctive
programs, which includes 0–1 programs, the convex hull with respect to $n$ disjunctions can
be built one disjunction at a time, in $n$ steps. Each step only needs the hull of a single
disjunction. This idea later became **lift-and-project**.

## Why it matters

- It explains *why* some MILP formulations are stronger than others: they are closer to
  the hull formulation.
- Lift-and-project and split cuts, standard in modern MILP solvers, trace back to these
  results.
- Generalized disjunctive programming [@raman1994] builds a modelling framework on top of it.
